text.hook:
Alignment questions look like trivia.
They are really about arrays, threads and wire formats.

Here is the mental model, plus 6 myths that fail interviews. Save it. 💡
text.body:
Inside:
1. sizeof vs alignof
2. Computing a layout by hand
3. What empty classes cost
4. Layout bugs only threads expose
5. Six myths, busted (slides 8-9)

Which myth did you believe? Comment the slide number.

slides.lead: Size vs alignment, how a layout is computed, and the layout bugs interviewers ask about.

slides.title: Every type has two numbers

cards.label: Size
cards.text: `sizeof(T)`: bytes the object occupies, padding included. Also the array stride.

cards.label: Alignment
cards.text: `alignof(T)`: every `T` address is a multiple of it. Always a power of two.

slides.takeaway: `sizeof` is always a multiple of `alignof`, but not equal: `struct { double d; char c; }` is size 16, alignment 8.

slides.title: What the ABI does, member by member
steps: For each member in declaration order: round the offset up to its alignment, place it, advance by its size.
Struct alignment = the largest member alignment.
Round the end up to that alignment: that is `sizeof` (tail padding).

slides.lead: `struct A { char c; int i; char d; }`: at 9 bytes, `arr[1].i` would sit at offset 13. Rounding up to 12 keeps every element aligned.

slides.title: What an empty `E` really costs
slides.takeaway: This is why `std::unique_ptr<T>` with a stateless deleter is 8 bytes. MSVC needs `[[msvc::no_unique_address]]`.

slides.title: Two layout bugs only threads expose

cards.label: False sharing
cards.text: Two threads write different variables on one 64-byte line: it bounces between cores. Fix: `alignas(64)` each hot variable.

cards.label: Bit-fields
cards.text: Adjacent bit-fields are **one** memory location. Two threads writing different fields: a data race (TSan reports it).

slides.takeaway: Cache-line padding wastes memory: use it for a few hot, contended objects, not for millions of small ones.

slides.title: Lock the layout at compile time
items: Fixed-width types: `long` is 4 bytes on 64-bit Windows, 8 on 64-bit Linux
slides.takeaway: A later edit that changes the layout now fails the build instead of corrupting data.

items.truth: By `alignof(T)`. A 12-byte struct with alignment 4 can start at address 100.

items.myth: "`sizeof(struct)` is a multiple of its largest member's size."
items.truth: It is a multiple of the struct's **alignment**.

items.myth: "The compiler reorders members to minimise padding."
items.truth: GCC, Clang and MSVC never reorder data members. Ordering them is your job.

items.myth: "Padding exists to keep a struct in one cache line."
items.truth: Padding satisfies alignment. Cache-line placement is a separate, explicit choice: `alignas(64)`.
It is UB in C++, slower across cache lines, non-atomic for atomics, and can fault on other CPUs.

items.myth: "Struct of arrays is always faster than array of structs."
items.truth: It depends on which fields the hot loop touches. Choose by access pattern.

slides.hero:
Offsets: multiples of
each member's alignment.

`sizeof`: rounded up to
the struct's alignment.
slides.lead: Save this. Follow for a C++ interview puzzle every day.

slides.title: Order members by decreasing alignment
slides.takeaway: One third less memory and more objects per cache line. Unless hot/cold grouping or ABI stability says otherwise.

text.body: One attribute, two compilers, two different reactions.

slides.title: What does GCC print? (x86-64)

slides.verdict_sub: GCC 11 and 13 compile it silently. Clang rejects it. The program is ill-formed.
bullets: Asking for less than the natural alignment (4, from `int`) is ill-formed.
Clang: "requested alignment is less than minimum alignment of 4".
So `value` stays at offset 4, and the size stays 8.

slides.title: `#pragma pack` really removes padding
slides.tip: The price: `value` is misaligned. Slower, non-atomic, and `&m.value` is a dangerous `int*`.

text.hook:
A packed struct saves 3 bytes per message.
GCC compiles it with -Wall -Wextra: zero warnings.

Lock in your answer below, then swipe ➜ to verify.
text.body: Packing shows up in every wire-format codebase. So does this bug.

slides.title: Which line is the bug?

bullets: `p.i`: the compiler knows `i` is packed and emits unaligned-safe code.
`q` claims to be an ordinary, aligned `int*`. Using it on a misaligned `i` is UB.
GCC 11 is silent here. UBSan at run time: "store to misaligned address".
Misaligned members also break atomics and SIMD, and fault on strict-alignment CPUs.

slides.title: Pack only at the I/O boundary
bullets: Reorder members first; pack only when an external byte format forces it.
slides.takeaway: Keep packing at the I/O boundary. Even there, `memcpy` into a naturally aligned struct is usually cleaner.

text.body: A one-liner that shows up in hash maps, caches and dedup code.

slides.title: Is `same()` a correct equality check?

slides.verdict_sub: `Key` is 12 bytes, but only 6 of them are data (x86-64)
bullets: Padding bytes have unspecified values: equal keys can compare different.
Aggregate `{}` init does not promise zeroed padding; copies need not keep it.
`memcmp` on a trivially copyable object is fine. The bytes are the problem.

slides.title: Compare members, not bytes
bullets: Byte-wise hashing has the same bug: equal keys, different buckets.
slides.takeaway: Writing a padded struct to a socket or file also leaks stale bytes.
